issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is poorly matched to the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. 'People in uniform' more strongly suggests assault/police/military trauma than a pediatric medical crisis, and there are no accompanying medical or hospital-related cues to make this clinically coherent.

issues.explanation: 'Revenge ... get even with assailant' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type because a child's life-threatening illness does not ordinarily involve an identifiable assailant. This item is therefore implausible for this trauma context.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'child's life-threatening illness,' revenge against an assailant is clinically incoherent because this trauma does not ordinarily involve a perpetrator to 'get even with.' A clinician would strongly question whether this item belongs to the same trauma narrative.

issues.item: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination implies a perpetrator/interpersonal harm frame ('what other people have done to me') that does not fit the listed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, unless there were unusual circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. This creates a hard-to-explain mismatch with the trauma context and with the trigger items, which are hospital/illness-related.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item about revenge against an assailant is not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, which does not normally involve a discrete assailant to get even with.

Together these maladaptive strategy items suggest an assault-like trauma narrative rather than a child's medical crisis.

issues.item: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination is possible in medical trauma, but in this profile it is framed as 'what other people have done to me,' which shifts the trauma narrative toward personal victimization rather than distress about a child's illness, making it hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

For trauma type 'child's life-threatening illness,' a burnt-smell danger cue is hard to reconcile clinically unless the illness involved fire/burning, which is not suggested by the trauma context. The hospital/antiseptic trigger fits, but burnt smell appears implausibly tied to a different trauma context.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Revenge against assailant' is strongly incongruent with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, which does not involve an assailant. This item implies an interpersonal assault/attack trauma and is not clinically coherent with the given trauma type.

issues.explanation: 'I dwell on what other people have done to me' similarly frames the trauma as interpersonal victimization by others, which is hard to reconcile with a child's medical crisis unless there were explicit malpractice/perpetrator elements, which are not present elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Leo, a 47-year-old South Eastern Asian man and married father of two, works as a park ranger in a large national forest. Four years ago, his then eight-year-old son was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The weeks that followed were a blur of hospital corridors, sterile antiseptic smells, and sleepless nights in hard plastic chairs. Leo remembers one night in particular: his son was febrile and neutropenic, and a resident came in with a faint trace of alcohol on his breath. Leo says nothing, but the smell lodged itself in his memory. He would later learn that the doctor had been off-duty hours earlier—still, the thought that someone less than fully present had touched his child’s IV line became a fixed point in his mind. The dizziness he now experiences began during that period—a sudden lightheadedness that would wash over him as he stood from his son’s bedside, the room tilting. Back then it was exhaustion and stress; now, even a mild spell of dizziness on the trail can stop him cold.

As a park ranger, Leo spends his days in open air, monitoring trails and assisting visitors. He avoids the ranger station when the staff restroom is being cleaned with antiseptic wipes—the scent of disinfectant pulls him back to the pediatric oncology floor. Alcohol smells are harder to escape. One of his colleagues brings craft beer to after-work bonfires; Leo has stopped attending entirely. When a hiker passes him with a flask, his jaw tightens. He has come to believe that the smell of alcohol was a sign of negligence, a betrayal of trust when his son needed vigilance most. But the trigger that most disrupts his work is dizziness. During a summer heatwave, he grew lightheaded while clearing a fallen branch. Instead of sitting down, he froze, his heart racing, convinced his body was repeating the same failure of control he felt in the hospital. He now carries a water bottle everywhere but still finds himself scanning for the first hint of imbalance.

Leo has developed a habit of dwelling on who was to blame for his son’s near-death experience. He spends hours mentally replaying the night that resident came in; he imagines confronting him, even getting even. He knows it is unrealistic—he never learned the man’s name—but the rumination feels like a kind of vigilance, a way of ensuring no one ever gets away with carelessness again. He also dwells on the attending physician who, in Leo’s view, dismissed his early concerns about his son’s bruising. “If I had pushed harder, if I had made them listen,” he tells his wife, replaying old arguments. But his wife avoids the topic now, and he takes that as further proof that no one understands the threat that still feels present.

These maladaptive strategies—the revenge fantasies, the bitterness toward the medical system—have the paradoxical effect of making his triggers more potent. On a morning when he wakes up already angry, the smallest whiff of antiseptic from a first-aid kit in his patrol vehicle will send him into a spiral. He connects the smell directly to the doctor’s breath, and that connection tightens his chest. He then feels the dizziness rising, as if the rage itself unsteadies him. He has come to believe that he must stay angry to stay safe, but the anger also keeps him primed to react to every somatic and olfactory reminder. The cycle has worn down his patience at work: his supervisor has noticed he snaps at visitors who approach him too quickly, or when a child’s cry echoes across a trailhead—sounds that remind him of his son’s pain.

Six months ago, Leo began avoiding any conversation that touches on illness or hospitals. When a friend called to say his brother had been diagnosed with cancer, Leo ended the call abruptly and hasn’t spoken to him since. His wife has started sleeping in the guest room because Leo wakes up thrashing, calling out for a nurse. He avoids looking at photos of his son from that year, and he has stopped attending family dinners where someone might ask, “How’s your boy now?” (The boy is in remission, healthy, but Leo cannot feel relief.) He has withdrawn so completely that his younger daughter asked him recently, “Dad, are you still mad at me?” That question, more than anything, brought him to the clinic. He is terrified that his rumination is poisoning the life he has now, but he also cannot shake the belief that if he stops watching, if he stops blaming, the next threat will already be in the room.
